theory.title: Variables in Robot Framework: Scalar Variables and Assignment
theory.content:
## Introduction to Variables

Variables are fundamental to any programming language, and Robot Framework is no exception. They allow you to **store data**, **reuse values**, and make your tests **data-driven** and **maintainable**. Understanding variable types and assignment is crucial for writing flexible, scalable test automation.

### Why Variables Matter

Without variables, tests become rigid and unmaintainable:

```robot
# Bad: Hardcoded values everywhere
*** Test Cases ***
Test User Login
    Open Browser    https://example.com    Chrome
    Input Text      id:username            admin@example.com
    Input Text      id:password            secret123
    
Test User Profile
    Open Browser    https://example.com    Chrome
    Input Text      id:username            admin@example.com
    Input Text      id:password            secret123
    Click Link      Profile
```

What happens when:
- The URL changes?
- The test user credentials change?
- You need to test against multiple environments?

You'd have to update **every occurrence** of these values—error-prone and time-consuming.

**With variables:**

```robot
*** Variables ***
${BASE_URL}       https://example.com
${USERNAME}       admin@example.com
${PASSWORD}       secret123

*** Test Cases ***
Test User Login
    Open Browser    ${BASE_URL}    Chrome
    Input Text      id:username    ${USERNAME}
    Input Text      id:password    ${PASSWORD}
    
Test User Profile
    Open Browser    ${BASE_URL}    Chrome
    Input Text      id:username    ${USERNAME}
    Input Text      id:password    ${PASSWORD}
    Click Link      Profile
```

Now you update **one place** and all tests reflect the change.

## Variable Types in Robot Framework

Robot Framework supports three primary variable types:

### 1. Scalar Variables

**Syntax:** `${variable_name}`

**Purpose:** Store a single value (string, number, object, etc.)

```robot
${name}        Set Variable    Robot
${count}       Set Variable    42
${pi}          Set Variable    3.14159
${flag}        Set Variable    ${True}
```

Scalar variables are the most common type and used for individual values.

### 2. List Variables

**Syntax:** `@{variable_name}`

**Purpose:** Store multiple values in an ordered collection

```robot
@{users}       Create List    alice    bob    charlie
@{numbers}     Create List    1        2      3        4
```

Access items:
```robot
Log    ${users}[0]    # Logs: alice
Log    ${users}[1]    # Logs: bob
```

### 3. Dictionary Variables

**Syntax:** `&{variable_name}`

**Purpose:** Store key-value pairs

```robot
&{user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    role=admin
```

Access values:
```robot
Log    ${user.name}    # Logs: John
Log    ${user}[age]    # Logs: 30
```

## The Set Variable Keyword

`Set Variable` is the most basic keyword for creating and assigning values to scalar variables at **runtime**.

### Syntax

```robot
${variable}    Set Variable    value
```

**Components:**
- `${variable}` — The variable to create/assign (leftmost position)
- `Set Variable` — The keyword name
- `value` — The value to assign (can be string, number, or another variable)

### How It Works

Robot Framework uses a **return value** pattern:

```robot
${result}    Keyword Name    arg1    arg2
```

The keyword executes, and its **return value** is assigned to the variable on the left.

For `Set Variable`, the return value is simply the argument you provide:

```robot
${name}    Set Variable    Robot
# ${name} now contains the string "Robot"
```

### Examples

**Assigning strings:**
```robot
${greeting}    Set Variable    Hello World
${status}      Set Variable    active
${path}        Set Variable    /home/user/data
```

**Assigning numbers:**
```robot
${count}       Set Variable    100
${price}       Set Variable    19.99
${quantity}    Set Variable    ${5}    # Explicit number type
```

**Assigning boolean values:**
```robot
${is_active}   Set Variable    ${True}
${has_error}   Set Variable    ${False}
```

**Assigning variables to variables:**
```robot
${original}    Set Variable    Robot Framework
${copy}        Set Variable    ${original}
Log            ${copy}    # Logs: Robot Framework
```

## Variable Scopes

Variables in Robot Framework have different **scopes** depending on where and how they're created.

### Test Scope (Default for Set Variable)

Variables created with `Set Variable` inside a test case are **test-scoped**:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test One
    ${var}    Set Variable    100
    Log       ${var}           # Works: 100

Test Two
    Log       ${var}           # FAILS: Variable ${var} not found
```

Each test starts with a **clean slate**—variables don't carry over.

### Suite Scope

Variables defined in `*** Variables ***` section are **suite-scoped**:

```robot
*** Variables ***
${SUITE_VAR}    Available to all tests

*** Test Cases ***
Test One
    Log    ${SUITE_VAR}    # Works

Test Two
    Log    ${SUITE_VAR}    # Works
```

Suite variables are available to **all test cases** in the file.

### Global Scope

Set variables globally using `Set Global Variable`:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test One
    Set Global Variable    ${GLOBAL_VAR}    I'm global

Test Two
    Log    ${GLOBAL_VAR}    # Works even though created in Test One
```

Global variables persist **across test cases** and **across suites** in the same execution.

**Use sparingly:** Global variables can make tests interdependent and harder to debug.

## Variable Naming Conventions

### Best Practices

**Use descriptive names:**
```robot
# Good
${user_email}       Set Variable    user@example.com
${api_timeout}      Set Variable    30
${expected_status}  Set Variable    200

# Poor
${x}     Set Variable    user@example.com
${t}     Set Variable    30
${s}     Set Variable    200
```

**Use UPPERCASE for constants (suite variables):**
```robot
*** Variables ***
${BASE_URL}        https://api.example.com
${MAX_RETRIES}     5
${TIMEOUT}         30
```

**Use lowercase for runtime variables:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
My Test
    ${response}     Make API Request
    ${user_count}   Get User Count
    ${is_valid}     Validate Response    ${response}
```

**Use underscores for readability:**
```robot
# Good
${user_profile}
${api_response_time}

# Harder to read
${userprofile}
${apiresponsetime}
```

## Type Handling in Robot Framework

Robot Framework is **dynamically typed**—variables can hold any Python type:

```robot
${string}    Set Variable    Hello
${number}    Set Variable    ${42}
${float}     Set Variable    ${3.14}
${bool}      Set Variable    ${True}
${none}      Set Variable    ${None}
```

### Implicit String Conversion

By default, Robot Framework treats values as **strings**:

```robot
${value}    Set Variable    42
# ${value} is the string "42", not the number 42
```

### Explicit Type Conversion

Use Python literals for non-string types:

```robot
${number}    Set Variable    ${42}        # Integer
${float}     Set Variable    ${3.14}      # Float
${bool}      Set Variable    ${True}      # Boolean
${list}      Set Variable    ${[1,2,3]}   # List
```

Alternatively, use `Convert To Integer`, `Convert To Number`, etc.:

```robot
${str_num}    Set Variable       42
${int_num}    Convert To Integer ${str_num}
```

## Logging Variables

The `Log` keyword outputs variable values to the execution log:

```robot
${name}    Set Variable    Robot Framework
Log        ${name}
```

**Output in log.html:**
```
INFO : Robot Framework
```

### Logging with Context

```robot
${count}    Set Variable    10
Log         The count is: ${count}
Log         Count=${count}, Status=Active
```

**Output:**
```
INFO : The count is: 10
INFO : Count=10, Status=Active
```

### Log Levels

```robot
Log    Normal message               # INFO (default)
Log    Debug message     DEBUG      # Only shown in debug mode
Log    Warning message   WARN       # Yellow in logs
Log    Error message     ERROR      # Red in logs
```

## Common Use Cases

### 1. Storing Keyword Return Values

```robot
${current_time}    Get Time
Log                ${current_time}

${length}          Get Length    ${some_list}
Should Be Equal    ${length}     ${5}
```

### 2. Intermediate Calculations

```robot
${price}        Set Variable    100
${quantity}     Set Variable    ${3}
${subtotal}     Evaluate        ${price} * ${quantity}
${tax}          Evaluate        ${subtotal} * 0.08
${total}        Evaluate        ${subtotal} + ${tax}
Log             Total: ${total}
```

### 3. Conditional Values

```robot
${env}     Set Variable    production
${url}     Set Variable If    '${env}' == 'production'    https://prod.com    https://dev.com
Log        Using URL: ${url}
```

### 4. Test Data Management

```robot
${test_user}    Set Variable    testuser@example.com
${test_pass}    Set Variable    SecurePassword123!
Login           ${test_user}    ${test_pass}
```

## Variable Substitution

Robot Framework performs **variable substitution** before executing keywords:

```robot
${name}    Set Variable    World
Log        Hello ${name}
```

**Execution steps:**
1. Robot Framework sees: `Log    Hello ${name}`
2. Substitutes `${name}` with `World`
3. Executes: `Log    Hello World`
4. Output: `Hello World`

### Nested Variables

```robot
${var_name}    Set Variable    greeting
${greeting}    Set Variable    Hello
Log            ${${var_name}}    # Logs: Hello
```

### Escaping Variables

To log literal `${variable}` without substitution:

```robot
Log    \${variable}    # Logs: ${variable}
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Initialize Variables Close to Usage

```robot
# Good: Clear and localized
*** Test Cases ***
User Registration Test
    ${email}       Set Variable    user@example.com
    ${password}    Set Variable    SecurePass123!
    Register User  ${email}    ${password}
```

### 2. Use Variables for Repeated Values

```robot
# Good: Easy to update
${base_url}    Set Variable    https://example.com
Open Browser   ${base_url}/login    Chrome
Go To          ${base_url}/profile
Go To          ${base_url}/settings
```

### 3. Avoid Magic Numbers

```robot
# Poor
Wait Until Element Is Visible    id:button    30

# Good
${timeout}    Set Variable    ${30}
Wait Until Element Is Visible    id:button    ${timeout}
```

### 4. Document Non-Obvious Values

```robot
# Timeout increased due to slow API response times
${api_timeout}    Set Variable    ${60}
```

## Common Pitfalls

### 1. Forgetting Variable Syntax

```robot
# Wrong: Missing ${}
name    Set Variable    Robot
Log     name    # Logs literal "name", not the value

# Correct
${name}    Set Variable    Robot
Log        ${name}    # Logs: Robot
```

### 2. Scope Confusion

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test One
    ${local_var}    Set Variable    100

Test Two
    Log    ${local_var}    # FAILS: Variable not found
```

### 3. Type Mismatches

```robot
${count}    Set Variable    10    # String "10"
${result}   Evaluate        ${count} + 5    # Error: can't concatenate string and int

# Fix: Explicit number
${count}    Set Variable    ${10}    # Integer 10
${result}   Evaluate        ${count} + 5    # Works: 15
```

## Summary

Variables in Robot Framework:
- **Store data** for reuse and flexibility
- Use `${name}` syntax for scalar variables
- Assign with `Set Variable` keyword
- Have different scopes (test, suite, global)
- Support all Python data types
- Are substituted before keyword execution
- Enable data-driven, maintainable tests

Mastering variables is the first step toward writing **flexible, maintainable, and scalable** test automation. As you progress, you'll use variables for test data, API responses, UI elements, and complex data structures—making them one of the most powerful features in Robot Framework.
learningObjectives: Understand the purpose and benefits of using variables in test automation
Create scalar variables using the Set Variable keyword
Use ${variable_name} syntax correctly
Log variable values to verify assignments and debug tests
Recognize different variable scopes (test, suite, global)

theory.title: String Manipulation and Variable Composition
theory.content:
## Working with Strings in Robot Framework

Strings are one of the most common data types in test automation—used for URLs, user inputs, expected messages, file paths, and more. Understanding how to **manipulate**, **combine**, and **transform** strings is essential for effective test automation.

### The Importance of String Operations

Consider these common testing scenarios:

**Scenario 1: Dynamic URLs**
```robot
${base_url}    Set Variable    https://api.example.com
${endpoint}    Set Variable    /users/123
${full_url}    Set Variable    ${base_url}${endpoint}
# Result: https://api.example.com/users/123
```

**Scenario 2: User Credentials**
```robot
${first_name}    Set Variable    John
${last_name}     Set Variable    Doe
${full_name}     Set Variable    ${first_name} ${last_name}
# Result: John Doe
```

**Scenario 3: Test Data Generation**
```robot
${timestamp}    Get Time    epoch
${username}     Set Variable    testuser_${timestamp}
# Result: testuser_1696284724
```

Without string manipulation, you'd need hardcoded values that can't adapt to different environments, data sets, or runtime conditions.

## String Concatenation with Set Variable

The simplest way to combine strings is using `Set Variable` with **variable substitution**.

### Basic Concatenation

```robot
${first}     Set Variable    Hello
${second}    Set Variable    World
${result}    Set Variable    ${first} ${second}
Log          ${result}    # Output: Hello World
```

**How it works:**
1. Robot Framework sees: `Set Variable    ${first} ${second}`
2. Substitutes variables: `Set Variable    Hello World`
3. Assigns result to `${result}`
4. `${result}` now contains: `Hello World`

### Concatenation Without Spaces

```robot
${protocol}    Set Variable    https://
${domain}      Set Variable    example.com
${url}         Set Variable    ${protocol}${domain}
Log            ${url}    # Output: https://example.com
```

No space between `${protocol}` and `${domain}`, so they're joined directly.

### Concatenation with Literals

```robot
${name}      Set Variable    Robot
${greeting}  Set Variable    Hello, ${name}!
Log          ${greeting}    # Output: Hello, Robot!
```

You can mix variables and literal text freely.

### Multiple Variables

```robot
${first}    Set Variable    Robot
${middle}   Set Variable    Framework
${last}     Set Variable    Testing
${full}     Set Variable    ${first} ${middle} ${last}
Log         ${full}    # Output: Robot Framework Testing
```

## Advanced String Operations

### Using the String Library

For complex string operations, Robot Framework provides the **String** library:

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library    String

*** Test Cases ***
String Operations
    ${result}    Replace String    Hello World    World    Robot
    Log          ${result}    # Output: Hello Robot
```

### Common String Keywords

**Replace String:**
```robot
${text}      Set Variable        The quick brown fox
${result}    Replace String      ${text}    fox    dog
Log          ${result}    # Output: The quick brown dog
```

**Convert To Uppercase:**
```robot
${text}      Set Variable            hello world
${upper}     Convert To Uppercase    ${text}
Log          ${upper}    # Output: HELLO WORLD
```

**Convert To Lowercase:**
```robot
${text}      Set Variable            HELLO WORLD
${lower}     Convert To Lowercase    ${text}
Log          ${lower}    # Output: hello world
```

**Get Substring:**
```robot
${text}      Set Variable      Robot Framework
${sub}       Get Substring     ${text}    0    5
Log          ${sub}    # Output: Robot
```

**Split String:**
```robot
${text}      Set Variable    apple,banana,cherry
@{fruits}    Split String    ${text}    ,
Log Many     @{fruits}       # Output: apple, banana, cherry
```

**Strip String (Remove Whitespace):**
```robot
${text}      Set Variable     "  hello  "
${clean}     Strip String     ${text}
Log          ${clean}    # Output: hello
```

**Should Contain:**
```robot
${text}    Set Variable    Robot Framework is awesome
Should Contain    ${text}    Framework    # Passes
```

## Variable Substitution in Depth

Variable substitution is **automatic** and happens **before** keywords execute.

### Substitution Order

```robot
${var1}    Set Variable    First
${var2}    Set Variable    ${var1} Second
${var3}    Set Variable    ${var2} Third
Log        ${var3}
```

**Execution flow:**
1. `${var1}` = `First`
2. `${var2}` = `First Second` (after substituting `${var1}`)
3. `${var3}` = `First Second Third` (after substituting `${var2}`)
4. Output: `First Second Third`

### Nested Substitution

```robot
${part}     Set Variable    name
${name}     Set Variable    Robot
${result}   Set Variable    ${${part}}
Log         ${result}    # Output: Robot
```

**How it works:**
1. Innermost substitution: `${part}` → `name`
2. Result: `${name}`
3. Second substitution: `${name}` → `Robot`
4. Final result: `Robot`

## String Formatting with Variables

### Template-Style Strings

```robot
${user}      Set Variable    Alice
${action}    Set Variable    logged in
${message}   Set Variable    User ${user} has ${action}
Log          ${message}    # Output: User Alice has logged in
```

### Building Complex Messages

```robot
${test_name}    Set Variable    Login Test
${status}       Set Variable    PASS
${duration}     Set Variable    2.5s
${report}       Set Variable    Test: ${test_name} | Status: ${status} | Duration: ${duration}
Log             ${report}
# Output: Test: Login Test | Status: PASS | Duration: 2.5s
```

## Real-World Use Cases

### 1. Dynamic API Endpoints

```robot
*** Variables ***
${BASE_API}    https://api.example.com/v1

*** Test Cases ***
Get User Data
    ${user_id}     Set Variable    12345
    ${endpoint}    Set Variable    ${BASE_API}/users/${user_id}
    ${response}    GET    ${endpoint}
    # Calls: https://api.example.com/v1/users/12345
```

### 2. Test Data Composition

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Create Test User
    ${timestamp}    Get Time      epoch
    ${email}        Set Variable  testuser_${timestamp}@example.com
    ${username}     Set Variable  user_${timestamp}
    Create User     ${username}   ${email}
    # Creates unique user: user_1696284724, testuser_1696284724@example.com
```

### 3. File Path Construction

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Upload Test File
    ${project_root}    Set Variable    /home/user/project
    ${test_data}       Set Variable    ${project_root}/test_data
    ${file_path}       Set Variable    ${test_data}/sample.csv
    Upload File        ${file_path}
    # Uploads: /home/user/project/test_data/sample.csv
```

### 4. Error Messages

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Response
    ${expected}    Set Variable    200
    ${actual}      Set Variable    404
    ${error_msg}   Set Variable    Expected status ${expected}, but got ${actual}
    Run Keyword If    '${actual}' != '${expected}'    Fail    ${error_msg}
    # Output: Expected status 200, but got 404
```

## String Comparison

### Case-Sensitive Comparison

```robot
${str1}    Set Variable    Hello
${str2}    Set Variable    hello
Should Be Equal    ${str1}    ${str2}    # FAILS: case mismatch
```

### Case-Insensitive Comparison

```robot
${str1}    Set Variable    Hello
${str2}    Set Variable    hello
Should Be Equal As Strings    ${str1}    ${str2}    ignore_case=True    # PASSES
```

### Partial String Matching

```robot
${text}    Set Variable    Robot Framework is great
Should Contain     ${text}    Framework       # PASSES
Should Start With  ${text}    Robot          # PASSES
Should End With    ${text}    great          # PASSES
```

## Using Evaluate for Complex Operations

For advanced string manipulation, use Python expressions:

```robot
${text}      Set Variable    hello world
${result}    Evaluate        '${text}'.upper()
Log          ${result}    # Output: HELLO WORLD

${joined}    Evaluate        '-'.join(['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'])
Log          ${joined}    # Output: apple-banana-cherry

${formatted}    Evaluate    f"User: {user}, Age: {age}"    user=Alice    age=30
Log             ${formatted}    # Output: User: Alice, Age: 30
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Use Descriptive Variable Names

```robot
# Good
${full_name}    Set Variable    ${first_name} ${last_name}

# Poor
${fn}    Set Variable    ${f} ${l}
```

### 2. Break Complex Concatenations into Steps

```robot
# Good: Clear and debuggable
${protocol}    Set Variable    https://
${domain}      Set Variable    api.example.com
${path}        Set Variable    /v1/users
${url}         Set Variable    ${protocol}${domain}${path}

# Poor: Hard to debug
${url}    Set Variable    https://api.example.com/v1/users
```

### 3. Use String Library for Complex Operations

```robot
# Good: Use appropriate keyword
${result}    Replace String    ${text}    old    new

# Poor: Manual replacement with Evaluate
${result}    Evaluate    '${text}'.replace('old', 'new')
```

### 4. Validate String Outputs

```robot
${full_name}    Set Variable    ${first} ${last}
Should Not Be Empty    ${full_name}
Should Match Regexp    ${full_name}    ^[A-Za-z ]+$
```

## Common Pitfalls

### 1. Forgetting Spaces in Concatenation

```robot
# Wrong: Missing space
${result}    Set Variable    ${first}${second}
# If first="Hello" and second="World", result="HelloWorld"

# Correct: Include space
${result}    Set Variable    ${first} ${second}
# Result: "Hello World"
```

### 2. Unintended Variable Substitution

```robot
# If you need literal "${variable}" in a string
${text}    Set Variable    The value is \${not_substituted}
Log        ${text}    # Output: The value is ${not_substituted}
```

### 3. Type Confusion

```robot
# String concatenation
${str1}    Set Variable    10
${str2}    Set Variable    20
${result}  Set Variable    ${str1}${str2}
# Result: "1020" (string concatenation, not addition)

# Numeric addition
${num1}    Set Variable    ${10}
${num2}    Set Variable    ${20}
${result}  Evaluate        ${num1} + ${num2}
# Result: 30 (numeric addition)
```

## Summary

String manipulation in Robot Framework:
- Use `Set Variable` for simple concatenation
- Combine variables and literals freely
- Use spacing to control output format
- Import String library for advanced operations
- Variable substitution is automatic
- Validate string outputs with assertions

Mastering string operations enables you to:
- Build dynamic test data
- Construct URLs, file paths, and messages
- Transform and validate text-based outputs
- Create flexible, data-driven tests

Strings are the **glue** that connects different parts of your tests, making string manipulation one of the most frequently used skills in test automation.
learningObjectives: Combine multiple variables into a single string using Set Variable
Understand how variable substitution works in string concatenation
Control spacing when combining strings
Use string composition to build dynamic test data

theory.title: List Variables and Collection Access in Robot Framework
theory.content:
## Introduction to List Variables

While scalar variables store **single values**, list variables store **multiple values** in an ordered collection. Lists are essential for working with datasets, iterating over items, and managing collections of test data.

### Why Lists Matter

Common testing scenarios that require lists:

**Scenario 1: Testing Multiple Users**
```robot
@{users}    Create List    alice    bob    charlie
FOR    ${user}    IN    @{users}
    Create Account    ${user}
END
```

**Scenario 2: Validating Multiple Elements**
```robot
@{required_fields}    Create List    username    email    password
FOR    ${field}    IN    @{required_fields}
    Page Should Contain Element    id:${field}
END
```

**Scenario 3: Processing API Response**
```robot
${response}     GET    /api/users
@{user_ids}     Get Value From JSON    ${response}    $..id
Log Many        @{user_ids}
```

Without lists, you'd need separate variables for each item—unmaintainable when dealing with dozens or hundreds of values.

## List Variable Syntax

List variables use the `@{variable_name}` syntax:

```robot
@{colors}    Create List    red    green    blue
```

**Key characteristics:**
- Prefix: `@{...}` for list variables
- Ordered: Items maintain insertion order
- Indexed: Access items by position (0-based)
- Mutable: Can add, remove, or modify items
- Heterogeneous: Can contain mixed types

## Creating Lists

### Using Create List Keyword

```robot
@{fruits}     Create List    apple    banana    orange
@{numbers}    Create List    1        2        3        4
@{mixed}      Create List    text     ${42}    ${True}
```

### Empty Lists

```robot
@{empty_list}    Create List
Log Many         @{empty_list}    # No output
```

### Lists in Variables Section

```robot
*** Variables ***
@{BROWSERS}       Chrome    Firefox    Edge
@{ENVIRONMENTS}   dev       staging    production
```

### Python-Style List Literals

```robot
@{items}    Set Variable    ${['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']}
```

## Accessing List Items

### Index-Based Access

Lists use **zero-based indexing**:

```robot
@{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana    orange

# Access by index
${first}     Set Variable   ${fruits}[0]     # apple
${second}    Set Variable   ${fruits}[1]     # banana
${third}     Set Variable   ${fruits}[2]     # orange
```

**Syntax:** `${list_name}[index]`

### Index Numbering

```
Index:     0        1         2
Item:    apple    banana    orange
```

First item is **always index 0**, not 1.

### Negative Indexing

Access items from the **end** of the list:

```robot
@{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana    orange

${last}       Set Variable   ${fruits}[-1]    # orange
${second_last} Set Variable  ${fruits}[-2]    # banana
${third_last}  Set Variable  ${fruits}[-3]    # apple
```

**Negative index mapping:**
```
Index:      -3       -2        -1
Item:     apple    banana    orange
```

Negative indexing is useful when you don't know the list length.

### Using Get From List Keyword

Alternative method from Collections library:

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library    Collections

*** Test Cases ***
List Access
    @{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana    orange
    ${first}     Get From List  ${fruits}    0
    Log          ${first}    # apple
```

**Difference:**
- `${list}[index]` — Direct syntax (inline)
- `Get From List` — Keyword-based (more explicit)

Both work identically; choose based on readability preference.

## List Slicing

Extract a **sublist** using slice notation:

```robot
@{numbers}    Create List    1    2    3    4    5
@{subset}     Evaluate       ${numbers}[1:4]
Log Many      @{subset}      # Output: 2, 3, 4
```

**Slice syntax:** `${list}[start:end]`
- `start` — Starting index (inclusive)
- `end` — Ending index (exclusive)

### Slice Examples

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c    d    e

# Get first 3 items
@{first_three}    Evaluate    ${items}[0:3]
# Result: [a, b, c]

# Get items from index 2 to end
@{from_middle}    Evaluate    ${items}[2:]
# Result: [c, d, e]

# Get items from start to index 3
@{to_middle}      Evaluate    ${items}[:3]
# Result: [a, b, c]

# Get every second item
@{every_second}   Evaluate    ${items}[::2]
# Result: [a, c, e]
```

## Working with Lists - Common Operations

### Get List Length

```robot
@{colors}    Create List    red    green    blue
${count}     Get Length     ${colors}
Log          ${count}    # Output: 3
```

### Append To List

```robot
@{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana
Append To List    ${fruits}    orange
Log Many     @{fruits}    # Output: apple, banana, orange
```

**Note:** `Append To List` modifies the list **in place**.

### Insert Into List

```robot
@{items}    Create List    first    third
Insert Into List    ${items}    1    second
Log Many    @{items}    # Output: first, second, third
```

### Remove Values From List

```robot
@{colors}    Create List    red    green    blue    red
Remove Values From List    ${colors}    red
Log Many     @{colors}    # Output: green, blue
```

Removes **all occurrences** of the value.

### Remove From List

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c
Remove From List    ${items}    1    # Remove item at index 1
Log Many    @{items}    # Output: a, c
```

### Reverse List

```robot
@{numbers}    Create List    1    2    3
Reverse List    ${numbers}
Log Many    @{numbers}    # Output: 3, 2, 1
```

### Sort List

```robot
@{names}    Create List    charlie    alice    bob
Sort List    ${names}
Log Many    @{names}    # Output: alice, bob, charlie
```

### List Should Contain Value

```robot
@{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana    orange
List Should Contain Value    ${fruits}    banana    # Passes
List Should Contain Value    ${fruits}    grape     # Fails
```

### Lists Should Be Equal

```robot
@{list1}    Create List    1    2    3
@{list2}    Create List    1    2    3
Lists Should Be Equal    ${list1}    ${list2}    # Passes
```

## Iterating Over Lists

Lists are commonly used with `FOR` loops:

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Process All Users
    @{users}    Create List    alice    bob    charlie
    FOR    ${user}    IN    @{users}
        Log    Processing user: ${user}
        Create Account    ${user}
    END
```

**Output:**
```
Processing user: alice
Processing user: bob
Processing user: charlie
```

### Enumerate with Index

```robot
@{items}    Create List    apple    banana    orange
${index}    Set Variable    ${0}
FOR    ${item}    IN    @{items}
    Log    Item ${index}: ${item}
    ${index}    Evaluate    ${index} + 1
END
```

**Output:**
```
Item 0: apple
Item 1: banana
Item 2: orange
```

## Expanding Lists in Keywords

Use `@{list}` to expand list items as separate arguments:

```robot
@{args}    Create List    arg1    arg2    arg3
My Keyword    @{args}
# Equivalent to: My Keyword    arg1    arg2    arg3
```

### Log Many Example

```robot
@{colors}    Create List    red    green    blue
Log Many     @{colors}
# Logs each color on a separate line
```

## Real-World Use Cases

### 1. Testing Multiple Browsers

```robot
@{browsers}    Create List    Chrome    Firefox    Edge
FOR    ${browser}    IN    @{browsers}
    Open Browser    https://example.com    ${browser}
    Page Should Contain    Welcome
    Close Browser
END
```

### 2. Validating Form Fields

```robot
@{required_fields}    Create List    username    email    password
FOR    ${field}    IN    @{required_fields}
    Element Should Be Visible    id:${field}
    Element Should Be Enabled    id:${field}
END
```

### 3. Processing API Response

```robot
${response}     GET              /api/products
@{product_ids}  Get Value From JSON    ${response}    $..id
FOR    ${id}    IN    @{product_ids}
    Log    Processing product: ${id}
END
```

### 4. Cleanup Operations

```robot
@{test_users}    Create List    user1    user2    user3

[Teardown]    Cleanup Test Users

*** Keywords ***
Cleanup Test Users
    FOR    ${user}    IN    @{test_users}
        Delete User    ${user}
    END
```

## List Variables in Variables Section

```robot
*** Variables ***
@{ENVIRONMENTS}       dev    staging    production
@{VALID_STATUSES}    200    201    204

*** Test Cases ***
Test API Across Environments
    FOR    ${env}    IN    @{ENVIRONMENTS}
        ${url}    Set Variable    https://${env}.example.com/api
        ${response}    GET    ${url}
        Should Be In List    ${response.status_code}    @{VALID_STATUSES}
    END
```

## Mixing Scalar and List Variables

```robot
${single_user}    Set Variable    admin
@{other_users}    Create List     alice    bob

# Combine in a new list
@{all_users}    Create List    ${single_user}    @{other_users}
Log Many        @{all_users}    # Output: admin, alice, bob
```

## Common Pitfalls

### 1. Index Out of Range

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c
${item}     Set Variable   ${items}[5]    # ERROR: Index 5 out of range
```

Always check list length before accessing:

```robot
${length}    Get Length    ${items}
Run Keyword If    ${length} > 5    Set Variable    ${items}[5]
```

### 2. Forgetting @ vs $ Prefix

```robot
# Wrong: Using scalar syntax for list
${fruits}    Create List    apple    banana
Log          ${fruits}[0]    # Works, but ${fruits} is actually a list

# Correct: Use list syntax
@{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana
Log          ${fruits}[0]    # Clearer intent
```

### 3. Modifying Lists During Iteration

```robot
# Dangerous: Modifying list while iterating
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c
FOR    ${item}    IN    @{items}
    Remove From List    ${items}    0    # Can cause unexpected behavior
END

# Better: Create a copy
@{items}        Create List    a    b    c
@{items_copy}   Copy List      ${items}
FOR    ${item}    IN    @{items_copy}
    # Process without modifying original
END
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Use Descriptive List Names

```robot
# Good
@{user_emails}
@{expected_statuses}
@{product_categories}

# Poor
@{list1}
@{data}
@{x}
```

### 2. Validate List Contents

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c
Should Not Be Empty    ${items}
${length}    Get Length    ${items}
Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${length}    3
```

### 3. Use Collections Library

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library    Collections

*** Test Cases ***
List Operations
    @{items}    Create List    item1    item2
    Append To List    ${items}    item3
    List Should Contain Value    ${items}    item2
```

## Summary

List variables in Robot Framework:
- Store **multiple values** in ordered collections
- Use `@{list_name}` syntax
- Access items with **zero-based indexing**: `${list}[0]`
- Support **negative indexing**: `${list}[-1]`
- Can be **modified** (append, remove, sort, reverse)
- Essential for **iteration** with FOR loops
- Expanded with `@{list}` in keyword arguments

Mastering lists enables you to:
- Process collections of test data
- Iterate over multiple scenarios
- Validate arrays of values
- Build flexible, data-driven tests

Lists are one of the most powerful features in Robot Framework, bridging the gap between simple scalar values and complex data structures.

Create lists using the Create List keyword
Access list items using zero-based indexing
Use negative indexing to access items from the end
Differentiate between scalar and list variable access patterns

theory.title: Collections Library and Advanced List Operations
theory.content:
## Introduction to the Collections Library

While Robot Framework's BuiltIn library provides basic variable handling, the **Collections library** offers powerful keywords for working with lists and dictionaries. This library is essential for advanced data manipulation in test automation.

### Importing Collections Library

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library    Collections
```

The Collections library is **standard** with Robot Framework (no pip install needed).

## List Manipulation Keywords

### Append To List

Adds an item to the **end** of a list:

```robot
@{items}    Create List    apple    banana
Append To List    ${items}    orange
Log Many    @{items}    # Output: apple, banana, orange
```

**Important:** Modifies the list **in place** (no return value).

**Syntax:**
```robot
Append To List    list    value1    value2    ...valueN
```

You can append **multiple values** at once:

```robot
@{numbers}    Create List    1    2
Append To List    ${numbers}    3    4    5
Log Many    @{numbers}    # Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
```

### Insert Into List

Inserts an item at a **specific index**:

```robot
@{items}    Create List    first    third
Insert Into List    ${items}    1    second
Log Many    @{items}    # Output: first, second, third
```

**Syntax:**
```robot
Insert Into List    list    index    value
```

### Remove Values From List

Removes **all occurrences** of specified values:

```robot
@{colors}    Create List    red    green    blue    red
Remove Values From List    ${colors}    red
Log Many    @{colors}    # Output: green, blue
```

Can remove multiple values:

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c    d    e
Remove Values From List    ${items}    b    d
Log Many    @{items}    # Output: a, c, e
```

### Remove From List

Removes an item at a **specific index**:

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c    d
Remove From List    ${items}    2    # Remove index 2 ("c")
Log Many    @{items}    # Output: a, b, d
```

Returns the removed value:

```robot
@{items}       Create List    x    y    z
${removed}     Remove From List    ${items}    1
Log            ${removed}    # Output: y
Log Many       @{items}      # Output: x, z
```

### Get Length

Returns the **number of items** in a collection:

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c    d
${count}    Get Length     ${items}
Log         ${count}    # Output: 4
```

Works with:
- Lists
- Dictionaries (returns number of key-value pairs)
- Strings (returns number of characters)

```robot
${text}      Set Variable    Robot Framework
${length}    Get Length      ${text}
Log          ${length}    # Output: 16
```

### Count Values In List

Counts **occurrences** of a value:

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    a    c    a
${count}    Count Values In List    ${items}    a
Log         ${count}    # Output: 3
```

### Get From List

Retrieves an item at a **specific index**:

```robot
@{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana    orange
${item}      Get From List  ${fruits}    1
Log          ${item}    # Output: banana
```

Equivalent to `${fruits}[1]` but more explicit.

### Get Slice From List

Extracts a **sublist**:

```robot
@{numbers}    Create List    1    2    3    4    5
@{subset}     Get Slice From List    ${numbers}    1    4
Log Many      @{subset}    # Output: 2, 3, 4
```

**Syntax:**
```robot
Get Slice From List    list    start_index    end_index
```

- `start_index` — Inclusive
- `end_index` — Exclusive

### Reverse List

Reverses the **order** of items:

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c
Reverse List    ${items}
Log Many    @{items}    # Output: c, b, a
```

**In-place operation** (modifies original list).

### Sort List

Sorts items in **ascending order**:

```robot
@{names}    Create List    charlie    alice    bob
Sort List    ${names}
Log Many    @{names}    # Output: alice, bob, charlie
```

Numeric sorting:

```robot
@{numbers}    Create List    10    2    30    1
Sort List    ${numbers}
Log Many    @{numbers}    # Output: 1, 2, 10, 30
```

### Copy List

Creates a **shallow copy** of a list:

```robot
@{original}    Create List    a    b    c
@{copy}        Copy List      ${original}
Append To List    ${copy}     d
Log Many       @{original}    # Output: a, b, c (unchanged)
Log Many       @{copy}        # Output: a, b, c, d
```

Useful when you need to modify a list without affecting the original.

## List Validation Keywords

### List Should Contain Value

Verifies a list contains a **specific value**:

```robot
@{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana    orange
List Should Contain Value    ${fruits}    banana    # Passes
List Should Contain Value    ${fruits}    grape     # Fails
```

### List Should Not Contain Value

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c
List Should Not Contain Value    ${items}    z    # Passes
```

### List Should Contain Sub List

Verifies a list contains **all items** from another list:

```robot
@{main_list}    Create List    a    b    c    d    e
@{sub_list}     Create List    b    d
List Should Contain Sub List    ${main_list}    ${sub_list}    # Passes
```

### Lists Should Be Equal

Compares two lists for **exact equality**:

```robot
@{list1}    Create List    1    2    3
@{list2}    Create List    1    2    3
Lists Should Be Equal    ${list1}    ${list2}    # Passes

@{list3}    Create List    3    2    1
Lists Should Be Equal    ${list1}    ${list3}    # Fails (different order)
```

### Should Be Empty

```robot
@{empty_list}    Create List
Should Be Empty    ${empty_list}    # Passes

@{items}    Create List    a
Should Be Empty    ${items}    # Fails
```

### Should Not Be Empty

```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b
Should Not Be Empty    ${items}    # Passes
```

## Real-World Use Cases

### 1. Managing Test Data

```robot
*** Variables ***
@{TEST_USERS}    user1    user2    user3

*** Test Cases ***
Setup Test Users
    FOR    ${user}    IN    @{TEST_USERS}
        Create User Account    ${user}
    END
    ${count}    Get Length    ${TEST_USERS}
    Log    Created ${count} test users
```

### 2. Processing API Response

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate User List
    ${response}     GET    /api/users
    @{user_ids}     Get Value From JSON    ${response}    $..id
    ${count}        Get Length    ${user_ids}
    Should Be True  ${count} > 0    msg=No users found
    List Should Contain Value    ${user_ids}    ${EXPECTED_USER_ID}
```

### 3. Dynamic Test Execution

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test Multiple Browsers
    @{browsers}    Create List    Chrome    Firefox
    Run Keyword If    ${INCLUDE_EDGE}    Append To List    ${browsers}    Edge
    FOR    ${browser}    IN    @{browsers}
        Open Browser    ${URL}    ${browser}
        Run Tests
        Close Browser
    END
```

### 4. Cleanup Operations

```robot
*** Variables ***
@{CREATED_RESOURCES}    Create List

*** Test Cases ***
Create Resources Test
    ${resource1}    Create Resource    Type1
    Append To List    ${CREATED_RESOURCES}    ${resource1}
    ${resource2}    Create Resource    Type2
    Append To List    ${CREATED_RESOURCES}    ${resource2}
    [Teardown]    Cleanup Created Resources

*** Keywords ***
Cleanup Created Resources
    FOR    ${resource}    IN    @{CREATED_RESOURCES}
        Delete Resource    ${resource}
    END
```

## Combining Keywords for Complex Operations

### Remove Duplicates

```robot
@{items}       Create List    a    b    a    c    b
@{unique}      Remove Duplicates    ${items}
Log Many       @{unique}    # Output: a, b, c
```

### Find Index of Item

```robot
@{fruits}    Create List    apple    banana    orange
${index}     Get Index From List    ${fruits}    banana
Log          ${index}    # Output: 1
```

Returns `-1` if item not found.

### Convert List to String

```robot
@{words}      Create List    Robot    Framework    Testing
${sentence}   Catenate    @{words}
Log           ${sentence}    # Output: Robot Framework Testing

# With custom separator
${csv}    Evaluate    ','.join(@{words})
Log       ${csv}    # Output: Robot,Framework,Testing
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Check List Length Before Access

```robot
@{items}    Get Items From Database
${count}    Get Length    ${items}
Run Keyword If    ${count} > 0    Process First Item    ${items}[0]
```

### 2. Use Validation Keywords

```robot
@{required_items}    Create List    item1    item2
@{actual_items}      Get Items From UI
List Should Contain Sub List    ${actual_items}    ${required_items}
```

### 3. Copy Lists Before Modification

```robot
@{original}    Get Test Data
@{working}     Copy List    ${original}
Append To List    ${working}    extra_item
# ${original} remains unchanged
```

### 4. Log List Contents for Debugging

```robot
@{items}    Get Items
Log Many    @{items}
${length}   Get Length    ${items}
Log         List contains ${length} items
```

## Summary

The Collections library provides:
- **Modification:** Append, Insert, Remove
- **Querying:** Get Length, Count Values, Get Index
- **Transformation:** Reverse, Sort, Copy, Slice
- **Validation:** Should Contain, Should Be Equal, Should Be Empty

These keywords enable:
- Dynamic test data management
- Complex data validation
- Flexible test workflows
- Robust collection handling

Mastering Collections library keywords is essential for working with realistic test data and building maintainable, data-driven test automation.
learningObjectives: Import and use the Collections library
Modify lists using Append To List and other manipulation keywords
Query list properties using Get Length and similar keywords
Understand in-place vs. copy-based list operations
Validate list contents with assertion keywords

theory.title: Dictionary Variables and Key-Value Data Structures
theory.content:
## Introduction to Dictionary Variables

Dictionaries (also called **maps** or **hash tables**) store data as **key-value pairs**. They're essential for representing structured data like user profiles, configuration settings, API responses, and test data.

### Why Dictionaries Matter

**Scenario 1: User Data**
```robot
&{user}    Create Dictionary    username=alice    email=alice@example.com    role=admin
Log        User: ${user.username}, Email: ${user.email}
```

**Scenario 2: API Request Body**
```robot
&{payload}    Create Dictionary    title=Test Post    body=Content here    userId=${1}
${response}   POST    /api/posts    json=${payload}
```

**Scenario 3: Configuration**
```robot
&{config}    Create Dictionary    timeout=30    retry=3    env=staging
${timeout}   Set Variable    ${config.timeout}
```

Dictionaries organize **related data** logically, making code readable and maintainable.

## Dictionary Variable Syntax

Dictionaries use the `&{variable_name}` syntax:

```robot
&{person}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30
```

**Key characteristics:**
- Prefix: `&{...}` for dictionary variables
- Unordered: Keys have no guaranteed order (Python 3.7+ maintains insertion order)
- Unique keys: Each key can appear only once
- Heterogeneous: Keys and values can be any type
- Mutable: Can add, remove, or modify entries

## Creating Dictionaries

### Using Create Dictionary Keyword

```robot
&{user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    active=${True}
```

**Syntax:** `key=value` pairs separated by spaces

### Empty Dictionaries

```robot
&{empty_dict}    Create Dictionary
Log    ${empty_dict}    # Output: {}
```

### Dictionaries in Variables Section

```robot
*** Variables ***
&{ADMIN}    username=admin    password=secret123    role=admin
&{CONFIG}   api_key=abc123    timeout=30
```

### Python-Style Dictionary Literals

```robot
&{data}    Evaluate    {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25}
```

## Accessing Dictionary Values

### Dot Notation

Most readable for known keys:

```robot
&{user}    Create Dictionary    name=John    email=john@example.com
Log        ${user.name}     # Output: John
Log        ${user.email}    # Output: john@example.com
```

**Syntax:** `${dict.key}`

### Bracket Notation

Required for dynamic keys or keys with special characters:

```robot
&{data}    Create Dictionary    user-name=John    item count=5
Log        ${data}[user-name]      # Output: John
Log        ${data}[item count]     # Output: 5
```

**Syntax:** `${dict}[key]`

### Using Get From Dictionary Keyword

Explicit keyword-based access:

```robot
&{config}    Create Dictionary    timeout=30    retry=3
${timeout}   Get From Dictionary  ${config}    timeout
Log          ${timeout}    # Output: 30
```

**Syntax:**
```robot
${value}    Get From Dictionary    dict    key
```

### Default Values

Return a default if key doesn't exist:

```robot
&{config}    Create Dictionary    timeout=30
${retry}     Get From Dictionary    ${config}    retry    ${5}
Log          ${retry}    # Output: 5 (default, since 'retry' key not found)
```

## Dictionary Manipulation Keywords

### Set To Dictionary

Adds or updates key-value pairs:

```robot
&{user}    Create Dictionary    name=John
Set To Dictionary    ${user}    age=30    email=john@example.com
Log    ${user}    # Output: {'name': 'John', 'age': 30, 'email': 'john@example.com'}
```

**In-place operation** (modifies original dictionary).

Can set multiple pairs:

```robot
Set To Dictionary    ${dict}    key1=value1    key2=value2    key3=value3
```

### Remove From Dictionary

Removes a key-value pair:

```robot
&{data}    Create Dictionary    a=1    b=2    c=3
Remove From Dictionary    ${data}    b
Log    ${data}    # Output: {'a': 1, 'c': 3}
```

Can remove multiple keys:

```robot
Remove From Dictionary    ${dict}    key1    key2    key3
```

### Get Dictionary Keys

Returns a list of all keys:

```robot
&{person}    Create Dictionary    name=Alice    age=25    city=NYC
@{keys}      Get Dictionary Keys   ${person}
Log Many     @{keys}    # Output: name, age, city
```

### Get Dictionary Values

Returns a list of all values:

```robot
&{scores}    Create Dictionary    math=90    english=85    science=92
@{values}    Get Dictionary Values    ${scores}
Log Many     @{values}    # Output: 90, 85, 92
```

### Get Dictionary Items

Returns a list of (key, value) tuples:

```robot
&{data}     Create Dictionary    a=1    b=2
@{items}    Get Dictionary Items  ${data}
Log Many    @{items}    # Output: a, 1, b, 2
```

### Dictionary Should Contain Key

Validates a key exists:

```robot
&{config}    Create Dictionary    host=localhost    port=8080
Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${config}    host    # Passes
Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${config}    username    # Fails
```

### Dictionary Should Contain Value

Validates a value exists:

```robot
&{settings}    Create Dictionary    theme=dark    language=en
Dictionary Should Contain Value    ${settings}    dark    # Passes
```

### Dictionary Should Contain Item

Validates a specific key-value pair:

```robot
&{user}    Create Dictionary    role=admin    status=active
Dictionary Should Contain Item    ${user}    role    admin    # Passes
```

### Dictionaries Should Be Equal

Compares two dictionaries:

```robot
&{dict1}    Create Dictionary    a=1    b=2
&{dict2}    Create Dictionary    a=1    b=2
Dictionaries Should Be Equal    ${dict1}    ${dict2}    # Passes
```

### Get Length

Returns the number of key-value pairs:

```robot
&{data}     Create Dictionary    x=10    y=20    z=30
${count}    Get Length    ${data}
Log         ${count}    # Output: 3
```

## Iterating Over Dictionaries

### Iterate Over Keys

```robot
&{scores}    Create Dictionary    math=90    english=85
@{keys}      Get Dictionary Keys   ${scores}
FOR    ${subject}    IN    @{keys}
    ${score}    Get From Dictionary    ${scores}    ${subject}
    Log    ${subject}: ${score}
END
```

### Iterate Over Items

```robot
&{config}    Create Dictionary    host=localhost    port=8080
@{items}     Get Dictionary Items  ${config}
FOR    ${key}    ${value}    IN    @{items}
    Log    ${key} = ${value}
END
```

## Real-World Use Cases

### 1. API Request/Response

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Create User Via API
    &{user_data}    Create Dictionary
    ...    username=testuser
    ...    email=test@example.com
    ...    password=SecurePass123!
    ...    role=user
    
    ${response}    POST    /api/users    json=${user_data}
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${response.status_code}    201
    
    &{response_body}    Set Variable    ${response.json()}
    Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${response_body}    id
    Should Be Equal    ${response_body.username}    testuser
```

### 2. Configuration Management

```robot
*** Variables ***
&{DEV_CONFIG}
...    api_url=https://dev.example.com
...    timeout=30
...    retry=3
...    debug=${True}

&{PROD_CONFIG}
...    api_url=https://api.example.com
...    timeout=60
...    retry=5
...    debug=${False}

*** Test Cases ***
Test With Environment Config
    ${env}        Get Environment Variable    ENV    default=dev
    &{config}     Set Variable If    '${env}' == 'prod'    ${PROD_CONFIG}    ${DEV_CONFIG}
    ${response}   GET    ${config.api_url}/health    timeout=${config.timeout}
```

### 3. User Profile Testing

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Update User Profile
    &{current_profile}    Get User Profile    user123
    Log    Current name: ${current_profile.name}
    
    &{updates}    Create Dictionary    name=New Name    bio=Updated bio
    Set To Dictionary    ${current_profile}    &{updates}
    
    Update User Profile    user123    ${current_profile}
    &{updated_profile}    Get User Profile    user123
    Should Be Equal    ${updated_profile.name}    New Name
```

### 4. Test Data Variants

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test Login Scenarios
    &{valid_user}      Create Dictionary    username=alice    password=correct123
    &{invalid_pass}    Create Dictionary    username=alice    password=wrong
    &{invalid_user}    Create Dictionary    username=nobody    password=anything
    
    Test Login Success     &{valid_user}
    Test Login Failure     &{invalid_pass}    expected_error=Invalid password
    Test Login Failure     &{invalid_user}    expected_error=User not found
```

## Nested Dictionaries

```robot
&{address}    Create Dictionary    street=123 Main St    city=NYC    zip=10001
&{user}       Create Dictionary    name=John    age=30    address=${address}

Log    ${user.name}              # Output: John
Log    ${user.address.city}      # Output: NYC
Log    ${user}[address][zip]     # Output: 10001
```

## Merging Dictionaries

```robot
&{dict1}    Create Dictionary    a=1    b=2
&{dict2}    Create Dictionary    c=3    d=4

# Merge dict2 into dict1
Set To Dictionary    ${dict1}    &{dict2}
Log    ${dict1}    # Output: {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3, 'd': 4}
```

## Common Pitfalls

### 1. Using Wrong Access Syntax

```robot
&{data}    Create Dictionary    user-name=John    item count=5

# Wrong: Dot notation doesn't work for keys with special characters
Log    ${data.user-name}    # ERROR

# Correct: Use bracket notation
Log    ${data}[user-name]    # Works
```

### 2. Forgetting & vs $ Prefix

```robot
# Wrong: Using scalar syntax
${user}    Create Dictionary    name=John

# Correct: Use dictionary syntax for clarity
&{user}    Create Dictionary    name=John
```

### 3. Key Not Found Errors

```robot
&{config}    Create Dictionary    timeout=30

# Fails if key doesn't exist
Log    ${config.retry}    # ERROR: Key 'retry' not found

# Better: Use Get From Dictionary with default
${retry}    Get From Dictionary    ${config}    retry    ${5}
Log         ${retry}    # Output: 5 (default)
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Use Descriptive Keys

```robot
# Good
&{user}    Create Dictionary    username=alice    email=alice@example.com

# Poor
&{user}    Create Dictionary    u=alice    e=alice@example.com
```

### 2. Validate Dictionary Structure

```robot
&{response}    Make API Request
Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${response}    status
Dictionary Should Contain Key    ${response}    data
Should Be Equal    ${response.status}    success
```

### 3. Use Dictionaries for Related Data

```robot
# Good: Group related fields
&{database}    Create Dictionary
...    host=localhost
...    port=5432
...    name=testdb
...    user=admin
...    password=secret

# Poor: Separate variables
${db_host}        Set Variable    localhost
${db_port}        Set Variable    5432
${db_name}        Set Variable    testdb
${db_user}        Set Variable    admin
${db_password}    Set Variable    secret
```

## Summary

Dictionary variables in Robot Framework:
- Store **key-value pairs** for structured data
- Use `&{dict_name}` syntax
- Access values via **dot notation** (`${dict.key}`) or **bracket notation** (`${dict}[key]`)
- Support **modification** (Set To Dictionary, Remove From Dictionary)
- Enable **validation** (Should Contain Key, Should Contain Item)
- Essential for **API testing**, **configuration**, and **complex test data**

Mastering dictionaries enables:
- Structured test data management
- API request/response handling
- Configuration-driven testing
- Complex data validation

Dictionaries, alongside lists, form the foundation of data-driven test automation in Robot Framework.

Create dictionaries using the Create Dictionary keyword
Access dictionary values using dot notation and bracket notation
Use Get From Dictionary with optional default values
Manipulate dictionaries with Set To Dictionary and Remove From Dictionary
relatedConcepts: Nested dictionaries and complex data structures

theory.title: Capturing Keyword Return Values and the Evaluate Keyword
theory.content:
## Return Values in Robot Framework

Most keywords in Robot Framework don't just perform actions—they also **return values**. Capturing these return values is essential for:
- Storing calculation results
- Validating API responses
- Extracting data from UI elements
- Chaining operations together

### The Return Value Pattern

```robot
${variable}    Keyword Name    arg1    arg2
```

**How it works:**
1. Keyword executes with provided arguments
2. Keyword completes and returns a value
3. Return value is assigned to `${variable}`
4. Variable can be used in subsequent keywords

### Examples of Keywords with Return Values

**Get Time:**
```robot
${timestamp}    Get Time    epoch
Log             ${timestamp}    # Output: 1696284724
```

**Get Length:**
```robot
@{items}    Create List    a    b    c
${count}    Get Length     ${items}
Log         ${count}    # Output: 3
```

**Get Element Text:**
```robot
${text}    Get Element Text    id:welcome-message
Log        ${text}    # Output: Welcome, User!
```

**API Request:**
```robot
${response}    GET    https://api.example.com/users/1
Log            ${response.status_code}    # Output: 200
```

## The Evaluate Keyword

`Evaluate` is a powerful keyword that executes **Python expressions** and returns the result. It's particularly useful for:
- Mathematical calculations
- String manipulation
- Type conversions
- Conditional logic
- Complex data transformations

### Syntax

```robot
${result}    Evaluate    expression
```

**Parameters:**
- `expression` — Any valid Python expression
- Returns the result of evaluating the expression

### Mathematical Operations

**Arithmetic:**
```robot
${sum}        Evaluate    10 + 5          # 15
${difference} Evaluate    20 - 8          # 12
${product}    Evaluate    10 * 5          # 50
${quotient}   Evaluate    100 / 4         # 25.0
${remainder}  Evaluate    17 % 5          # 2
${power}      Evaluate    2 ** 8          # 256
```

**Complex expressions:**
```robot
${result}    Evaluate    (10 + 5) * 2 - 8    # 22
${avg}       Evaluate    (90 + 85 + 92) / 3  # 89.0
```

**Using variables:**
```robot
${price}      Set Variable    ${100}
${quantity}   Set Variable    ${3}
${total}      Evaluate        ${price} * ${quantity}
Log           ${total}    # Output: 300
```

### String Operations

**Case conversion:**
```robot
${text}      Set Variable    hello world
${upper}     Evaluate        '${text}'.upper()
Log          ${upper}    # Output: HELLO WORLD

${lower}     Evaluate        '${text}'.lower()
Log          ${lower}    # Output: hello world
```

**String methods:**
```robot
${text}       Set Variable    Robot Framework
${replaced}   Evaluate        '${text}'.replace('Robot', 'Python')
Log           ${replaced}    # Output: Python Framework

${split}      Evaluate        '${text}'.split()
Log Many      @{split}       # Output: Robot, Framework

${joined}     Evaluate        '-'.join(['a', 'b', 'c'])
Log           ${joined}      # Output: a-b-c
```

### Boolean and Comparison Operations

```robot
${is_greater}    Evaluate    10 > 5           # True
${is_equal}      Evaluate    5 == 5           # True
${is_not_equal}  Evaluate    'a' != 'b'       # True
${and_result}    Evaluate    True and False   # False
${or_result}     Evaluate    True or False    # True
```

### Conditional Expressions

```robot
${score}    Set Variable    ${85}
${grade}    Evaluate        'Pass' if ${score} >= 60 else 'Fail'
Log         ${grade}    # Output: Pass

${status}   Evaluate    'Adult' if ${age} >= 18 else 'Minor'
```

### Type Conversions

```robot
${str_num}    Set Variable       42
${int_num}    Evaluate           int('${str_num}')
${float_num}  Evaluate           float('3.14')
${str_val}    Evaluate           str(${int_num})
```

### List and Dictionary Operations

**List comprehensions:**
```robot
${squared}    Evaluate    [x**2 for x in range(5)]
Log Many      @{squared}  # Output: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16
```

**Dictionary creation:**
```robot
&{user}    Evaluate    {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30, 'active': True}
Log        ${user.name}    # Output: Alice
```

### Using Python Modules

Import and use Python standard library modules:

```robot
# Math module
${sqrt}    Evaluate    math.sqrt(16)    modules=math
Log        ${sqrt}    # Output: 4.0

${ceil}    Evaluate    math.ceil(4.3)   modules=math
Log        ${ceil}    # Output: 5

# Random module
${rand}    Evaluate    random.randint(1, 100)    modules=random
Log        Random number: ${rand}

# Datetime module
${now}     Evaluate    datetime.datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d')    modules=datetime
Log        ${now}    # Output: 2025-10-02
```

### Passing Variables to Evaluate

Use keyword arguments for cleaner expressions:

```robot
${result}    Evaluate    x * y + z    x=${10}    y=${5}    z=${3}
Log          ${result}    # Output: 53

${greeting}  Evaluate    f"Hello, {name}!"    name=Alice
Log          ${greeting}    # Output: Hello, Alice!
```

## Numeric Comparisons

### Should Be Equal with Numbers

When comparing numbers, Robot Framework's type handling matters:

**String comparison (default):**
```robot
${result}    Evaluate    10 * 5
Should Be Equal    ${result}    50    # May fail due to type mismatch
```

**Explicit number comparison:**
```robot
${result}    Evaluate    10 * 5
Should Be Equal    ${result}    ${50}    # Using ${} for integer type
```

**Or use specialized keyword:**
```robot
${result}    Evaluate    10 * 5
Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${result}    50    # Type-aware comparison
```

### Should Be Equal As Numbers

Compares values as numbers, regardless of type:

```robot
${calc}    Evaluate    10 * 5
Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${calc}    50      # Passes
Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${calc}    50.0    # Passes
Should Be Equal As Numbers    50         50      # Passes
```

### Should Be Equal As Integers

Strict integer comparison:

```robot
${value}    Evaluate    int(42.7)
Should Be Equal As Integers    ${value}    42    # Passes
```

## Real-World Use Cases

### 1. Calculating Expected Values

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Cart Total
    ${item1_price}    Set Variable    ${29.99}
    ${item2_price}    Set Variable    ${49.99}
    ${item1_qty}      Set Variable    ${2}
    ${item2_qty}      Set Variable    ${1}
    
    ${subtotal}       Evaluate        ${item1_price} * ${item1_qty} + ${item2_price} * ${item2_qty}
    ${tax}            Evaluate        ${subtotal} * 0.08
    ${expected_total} Evaluate        ${subtotal} + ${tax}
    
    ${actual_total}   Get Cart Total From UI
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${actual_total}    ${expected_total}
```

### 2. Dynamic Test Data Generation

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Create Unique User
    ${timestamp}    Evaluate    int(time.time())    modules=time
    ${username}     Set Variable    user_${timestamp}
    ${email}        Set Variable    user_${timestamp}@example.com
    
    Create User Account    ${username}    ${email}
```

### 3. Date/Time Calculations

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Validate Future Date
    ${today}         Evaluate    datetime.date.today()    modules=datetime
    ${future_date}   Evaluate    ${today} + datetime.timedelta(days=30)    modules=datetime
    ${formatted}     Evaluate    ${future_date}.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')    modules=datetime
    
    Log    Expiration date: ${formatted}
```

### 4. Conditional Test Logic

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Conditional Execution
    ${env}           Get Environment Variable    ENV    default=dev
    ${timeout}       Evaluate    60 if '${env}' == 'prod' else 30
    ${retries}       Evaluate    5 if '${env}' == 'prod' else 3
    
    Make API Request    timeout=${timeout}    retry=${retries}
```

### 5. Parsing and Extracting Data

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Extract User ID from URL
    ${url}       Set Variable    https://example.com/users/12345/profile
    ${user_id}   Evaluate        '${url}'.split('/')[-2]
    Log          User ID: ${user_id}    # Output: 12345
```

## When to Use Evaluate

### Good Use Cases
- Mathematical calculations
- Date/time operations
- String transformations
- Type conversions
- Simple Python expressions

### When to Avoid
- Complex logic (use custom Python keywords instead)
- Business logic (should be in application, not tests)
- Security-sensitive operations (validate inputs)
- When specialized keywords exist (prefer built-in)

## Security Considerations

`Evaluate` executes **arbitrary Python code**, so:
- Never evaluate **untrusted user input**
- Avoid in production environments with external data
- Prefer type-safe keywords when available

```robot
# Dangerous: Evaluating user input
${user_input}    Get User Input
${result}        Evaluate    ${user_input}    # Can execute malicious code!

# Better: Validate first
${safe_number}   Convert To Integer    ${user_input}
${result}        Evaluate               ${safe_number} * 2
```

## Best Practices

### 1. Use Variables for Clarity

```robot
# Good: Clear intermediate steps
${price}      Set Variable    ${100}
${quantity}   Set Variable    ${3}
${discount}   Set Variable    ${0.10}
${subtotal}   Evaluate        ${price} * ${quantity}
${total}      Evaluate        ${subtotal} * (1 - ${discount})

# Poor: Complex one-liner
${total}    Evaluate    100 * 3 * (1 - 0.10)
```

### 2. Prefer Specialized Keywords

```robot
# Good: Use built-in keyword
${length}    Get Length    ${list}

# Poor: Using Evaluate unnecessarily
${length}    Evaluate    len(${list})
```

### 3. Document Complex Expressions

```robot
# Calculate compound interest: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt)
${amount}    Evaluate    ${principal} * (1 + ${rate}/${compounding_periods}) ** (${compounding_periods} * ${years})
```

## Summary

Keyword return values:
- Most keywords **return values** that can be captured
- Use `${variable}    Keyword    args` pattern
- Essential for chaining operations and validation

The Evaluate keyword:
- Executes **Python expressions**
- Returns the **result** for assignment
- Supports **arithmetic**, **string operations**, **conditionals**
- Can import **Python modules**
- Useful for **calculations** and **transformations**
- Use with **caution** (arbitrary code execution)

Numeric comparison:
- Use `${number}` syntax for type-aware values
- Use `Should Be Equal As Numbers` for numeric assertions
- Avoid string comparison for numeric values

Mastering return values and `Evaluate` enables sophisticated test logic, dynamic data generation, and complex validations—all while keeping tests readable and maintainable.
learningObjectives: Understand how keywords return values and how to capture them
Use the Evaluate keyword to execute Python expressions
Perform mathematical calculations within test cases
Compare numeric values using appropriate assertion keywords
Apply the return value pattern to chain operations

theory.title: Robot Framework Built-In Variables and System Information
theory.content:
## Introduction to Built-In Variables

Robot Framework provides a set of **built-in variables** that are automatically available in all test suites without any configuration. These variables provide access to:
- File system paths
- Execution context information
- Operating system details
- Special characters and constants

### Why Built-In Variables Matter

Built-in variables enable **portable, cross-platform tests**:

**Without built-in variables:**
```robot
# Hard-coded Windows path - fails on Linux/Mac
${file_path}    Set Variable    C:\Users\test\data\input.txt

# Hard-coded path separator - not portable
${config_file}    Set Variable    configs\test.yaml
```

**With built-in variables:**
```robot
# Portable across all operating systems
${file_path}    Set Variable    ${CURDIR}${/}data${/}input.txt
${config_file}  Set Variable    ${CURDIR}${/}configs${/}test.yaml
```

Built-in variables make tests **resilient** to different environments and platforms.

## Path-Related Built-In Variables

### ${CURDIR} - Current Directory

The **absolute path** to the directory where the current test suite file is located.

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Current Directory
    Log    ${CURDIR}
    # Output (example): /home/user/project/tests
```

**Use cases:**
- Loading test data files relative to suite location
- Constructing paths to resources
- Referencing configuration files

**Example:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Load Test Data
    ${data_file}    Set Variable    ${CURDIR}${/}test_data${/}users.csv
    @{users}        Load CSV         ${data_file}
```

### ${EXECDIR} - Execution Directory

The **absolute path** to the directory where test execution was **started** (where `robot` command was run).

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Execution Directory
    Log    ${EXECDIR}
    # Output (example): /home/user/project
```

**Difference from ${CURDIR}:**
- `${CURDIR}` — Where the **.robot file** is located
- `${EXECDIR}` — Where the **robot command** was executed

**Use cases:**
- Accessing project-level configuration
- Finding files relative to project root
- Portable CI/CD configurations

### ${OUTPUT_DIR} - Output Directory

The **absolute path** to the directory where **output files** (log.html, report.html, output.xml) are written.

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Output Directory
    Log    ${OUTPUT_DIR}
    # Output (example): /home/user/project/results
```

**Use cases:**
- Saving screenshots in output directory
- Creating additional artifacts
- Referencing output files in teardown

**Example:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Capture Screenshot On Failure
    Run Keyword And Return Status    Some Keyword That Might Fail
    Run Keyword If    '${TEST_STATUS}' == 'FAIL'
    ...    Capture Page Screenshot    ${OUTPUT_DIR}${/}failure_${TEST_NAME}.png
```

### ${TEMPDIR} - Temporary Directory

The **system's temporary directory** path (OS-dependent).

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Temp Directory
    Log    ${TEMPDIR}
    # Output (example): /tmp (Linux/Mac) or C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp (Windows)
```

**Use cases:**
- Creating temporary test files
- Storing intermediate data
- Cleanup operations

**Example:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Create Temp File
    ${temp_file}    Set Variable    ${TEMPDIR}${/}test_${SUITE_NAME}.txt
    Create File     ${temp_file}    Test data
    [Teardown]      Remove File    ${temp_file}
```

### ${/} - Path Separator

The **operating system's path separator** character:
- `/` on Unix/Linux/Mac
- `\` on Windows

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Path Separator
    Log    ${/}
    # Output: / (on Linux/Mac) or \ (on Windows)
```

**Use cases:**
- Building cross-platform file paths
- Joining path components
- Portable directory structures

**Example:**
```robot
*** Variables ***
${CONFIG_FILE}    ${CURDIR}${/}configs${/}settings.yaml
${DATA_DIR}       ${EXECDIR}${/}test_data${/}api
```

### ${:} - Path Component Separator

The **path list separator** used in environment variables like `PATH`:
- `:` on Unix/Linux/Mac
- `;` on Windows

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Path Component Separator
    Log    ${:}
    # Output: : (on Linux/Mac) or ; (on Windows)
```

**Use cases:**
- Parsing PATH environment variable
- Building classpath or library paths

## Execution Context Variables

### ${SUITE_NAME}

The **name** of the current test suite.

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Suite Name
    Log    ${SUITE_NAME}
    # Output: My Test Suite
```

### ${SUITE_SOURCE}

The **absolute path** to the suite file.

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Suite Source
    Log    ${SUITE_SOURCE}
    # Output: /home/user/project/tests/login_tests.robot
```

### ${TEST_NAME}

The **name** of the currently executing test case.

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Test Name
    Log    ${TEST_NAME}
    # Output: Show Test Name
```

**Use case:**
```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Test With Unique Screenshot
    Run Some Test Steps
    Capture Page Screenshot    ${OUTPUT_DIR}${/}${TEST_NAME}.png
```

### ${LOG_LEVEL}

The current **log level** (TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR).

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Show Log Level
    Log    ${LOG_LEVEL}
    # Output: INFO (default)
```

## Special Character Variables

### ${SPACE}

A single **space character**.

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Use Space Variable
    ${text}    Set Variable    Hello${SPACE}World
    Log        ${text}    # Output: Hello World
```

**Use case:** When you need explicit spacing in strings.

### ${EMPTY}

An **empty string** (`''`).

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Use Empty Variable
    ${var}    Set Variable    ${EMPTY}
    Should Be Equal    ${var}    ${EMPTY}
    Should Be Empty    ${var}
```

**Use cases:**
- Checking for empty values
- Initializing optional parameters
- Clearing fields

### ${True} and ${False}

Boolean **true** and **false** values.

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Use Boolean Variables
    ${is_active}    Set Variable    ${True}
    ${is_deleted}   Set Variable    ${False}
    
    Run Keyword If    ${is_active}    Log    User is active
    Should Be True    ${is_active}
```

### ${None}

Python's **None** value (null).

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Use None Variable
    ${result}    Set Variable    ${None}
    Should Be Equal    ${result}    ${None}
    Run Keyword If    ${result} is None    Log    Result is None
```

## Number Variables

### ${0} through ${9}

Integer values **0-9** (rarely needed, but available).

```robot
*** Test Cases ***
Use Number Variables
    ${zero}    Set Variable    ${0}
    ${five}    Set Variable    ${5}
    Should Be Equal As Numbers    ${zero}    0
```

## Operating System Variables

## Best Practices

### 1. Always Use ${/} for Paths

```robot
# Good: Cross-platform
${path}    Set Variable    ${CURDIR}${/}data${/}file.txt

# Bad: Windows-only
${path}    Set Variable    ${CURDIR}\data\file.txt

# Bad: Unix-only
${path}    Set Variable    ${CURDIR}/data/file.txt
```

### 2. Use ${CURDIR} for Suite-Relative Resources

```robot
# Good: Relative to suite location
Resource    ${CURDIR}${/}..${/}resources${/}common.robot

# Poor: Absolute path (not portable)
Resource    /home/user/project/resources/common.robot
```

### 3. Use ${OUTPUT_DIR} for Test Artifacts

```robot
# Good: Saves to output directory
Capture Page Screenshot    ${OUTPUT_DIR}${/}failure.png

# Poor: Hard-coded path
Capture Page Screenshot    /tmp/failure.png
```

### 4. Document Custom Path Variables

```robot
*** Variables ***
# Test data directory relative to suite location
${TEST_DATA}    ${CURDIR}${/}test_data

# Configuration file at project root
${CONFIG}       ${EXECDIR}${/}config.yaml
```

## Common Pitfalls

### 1. Confusing ${CURDIR} and ${EXECDIR}

```robot
# ${CURDIR} - where the .robot file is
# ${EXECDIR} - where 'robot' command was run

# If running: robot tests/login_tests.robot
# ${CURDIR} = /project/tests
# ${EXECDIR} = /project
```

### 2. Forgetting ${/} in Paths

```robot
# Wrong: Missing separator
${path}    Set Variable    ${CURDIR}data${/}file.txt
# Result: /project/testsdata/file.txt (wrong!)

# Correct:
${path}    Set Variable    ${CURDIR}${/}data${/}file.txt
# Result: /project/tests/data/file.txt
```

### 3. Hard-Coding Paths

```robot
# Avoid:
${log_file}    Set Variable    C:\logs\test.log

# Better:
${log_file}    Set Variable    ${OUTPUT_DIR}${/}test.log
```

## Summary

Built-in variables in Robot Framework:
- **Always available** without configuration
- Provide **system information** and **paths**
- Enable **cross-platform compatibility**
- Include **special characters** and **constants**

Key built-in variables:
- `${CURDIR}` — Suite file directory
- `${EXECDIR}` — Execution directory
- `${OUTPUT_DIR}` — Output files directory
- `${TEMPDIR}` — System temp directory
- `${/}` — Path separator
- `${SPACE}`, `${EMPTY}`, `${True}`, `${False}`, `${None}` — Special values

Mastering built-in variables enables:
- **Portable tests** across Windows/Linux/Mac
- **Flexible resource management**
- **Clean artifact organization**
- **Environment-agnostic test design**

Built-in variables are the foundation of **maintainable, portable Robot Framework test suites**.
